_comment: Cambridge English Qualifications: B1 Preliminary, B2 First and C1 Advanced. EVERY figure verified from Cambridge English's own pages: the exam-format page for each qualification (cambridgeenglish.org/exams-and-tests/<name>/exam-format/) for papers, durations, parts, questions and any printed weighting, and the shared results page (cambridgeenglish.org/exams-and-tests/qualifications/results/) for the grade tables. NOTE ON WEIGHTINGS: the B1 Preliminary format page prints 25% against each of its four papers. The B2 First format page prints 40% against Reading and Use of English and 20% against Writing, and prints NO weighting against Listening or Speaking; the C1 Advanced format page prints no weightings at all. The five-component averaging model - Reading, Use of English, Writing, Listening and Speaking equally weighted at 20% each - is Cambridge's own published scoring model, and is what reconciles the 40%. Pages say which figure came from where. Nothing of Cambridge's is reproduced beyond short factual phrases: no question, task or mark-scheme wording is copied, and all method is RCF English's own.

hero.text: Four papers, four equal quarters. The cleanest arithmetic on the whole Cambridge ladder, and the level at which everyday English becomes a certificate.

blocks.title: Where these figures come from
text: Papers, durations, parts, questions and weightings were read from Cambridge English's own [B1 Preliminary exam format page](https://www.cambridgeenglish.org/exams-and-tests/preliminary/exam-format/). The grade table was read from Cambridge's [results page](https://www.cambridgeenglish.org/exams-and-tests/qualifications/results/).

Cambridge materials are linked, never copied. No question, task or mark-scheme wording is reproduced; the methods on this page are RCF English's own. **RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Cambridge English.**

blocks.heading: The four papers
rows: 10-12 minutes per pair of candidates; 15-17 minutes per group of three

blocks.title: Four skills, four equal quarters
text: B1 Preliminary is the straightforward one. **Each of the four papers is worth exactly 25%**, and your overall score is the average of the four.

This matters because it makes neglect expensive in a way candidates underestimate. Speaking is a quarter of the qualification and takes eleven minutes; Reading is a quarter and takes forty-five. **A candidate who never practises speaking has given away as much as one who never practises reading.**

It also differs from the levels above it. At B2 First and C1 Advanced there are **five** scored components, not four, because Use of English is counted separately. Do not carry the arithmetic from one level to the next.

blocks.heading: Grades and what they certify
blocks.caption: Scores as published by Cambridge English. B1 Preliminary is a B1 examination, so Grade A certifies a level above the one you entered for, and a score in the lowest band certifies the level below.

blocks.title: The two things this table is telling you
text: **You can pass upwards.** A score of 160 or above on a B1 examination earns a certificate stating B2. That is a real result, not a consolation, and for some candidates it is a cheaper route to a B2 certificate than entering B2 First and failing it.

**You can pass downwards.** A score between 120 and 139 still produces a certificate, at A2. You are not left with nothing, which is the fear that pushes candidates into entering a level below the one they could reach.

parts.heading: Reading: 45 minutes, 6 parts, 32 questions
bullets: **Forty-five minutes for thirty-two questions is about eighty seconds each**, and the parts are not equally hard. Move on from anything that has taken two minutes and come back.
The parts move from short notices and messages towards longer continuous texts. **Do the short parts quickly and buy yourself time for the long ones**, not the other way round.
**Answer every question.** There is no penalty for a wrong answer at this level, so a blank is a guaranteed nought and a guess is not.
Practise with a clock from the start. Candidates rarely fail this paper on comprehension; they fail it on the last six questions.

parts.heading: Writing: 45 minutes, 2 parts
bullets: Two pieces in forty-five minutes means about **twenty minutes each, with five to check**. The checking is not optional at this level - it is where the easy marks are.
**Answer the question that was set.** The commonest way to lose marks here is a well-written piece that covers two of the three things asked for.
**Hold the register.** An email to a friend and a piece written for a teacher do not sound the same, and the difference is assessed.
**Length is a guide, not a target.** Going far over costs time and adds errors; going far under leaves content marks unclaimed.

parts.heading: Listening: 30 minutes, 4 parts, 25 questions
bullets: **Six of those thirty minutes are transfer time**, so the listening itself is shorter than the figure suggests. Know that before the day.
**Read the questions in the pause before each part.** Knowing what you are listening for is most of this paper.
**You hear everything twice.** Use the first listening for the answer and the second for the ones you missed, rather than trying to be certain first time.
**Write something for every question**, even on the first listening. An answer you improve is better than a blank you run out of time to fill.

parts.heading: Speaking: 10-12 minutes, 4 parts
bullets: You are examined **with a partner**, and part of what is assessed is how you interact with them. **Listen and respond** rather than delivering a prepared turn.
**Do not rescue a silent partner by talking over them**, and do not go quiet if they dominate. The examiner is assessing you, and both extremes cost you.
**Extend your answers.** A one-word answer gives the assessor nothing to credit. Give the answer, then a reason or an example.
**Accuracy matters less than range and communication at this level.** Say the more interesting thing imperfectly rather than the dull thing safely.
It is a quarter of the qualification and it is over in eleven minutes. Practise it out loud with somebody, not silently in your head.

hero.text: Four papers, but five scored components. The one arithmetic fact that changes how you should revise for this examination.

blocks.title: Where these figures come from
text: Papers, durations, parts and questions were read from Cambridge English's own [B2 First exam format page](https://www.cambridgeenglish.org/exams-and-tests/first/exam-format/). The grade table was read from Cambridge's [results page](https://www.cambridgeenglish.org/exams-and-tests/qualifications/results/).

**A note on the weightings.** Cambridge's format page prints **40%** against Reading and Use of English and **20%** against Writing. It prints no percentage against Listening or Speaking. The five-component model described below is Cambridge's own published scoring method, and it is what reconciles the 40%.

Cambridge materials are linked, never copied. No question, task or mark-scheme wording is reproduced; the methods on this page are RCF English's own. **RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Cambridge English.**

blocks.heading: The four papers
rows: 2 parts - Part 1 one compulsory question, Part 2 one question from a choice of four

blocks.title: Four papers, five scores - and this is the thing to understand
text: Your overall result is **the average of five separate component scores: Reading, Use of English, Writing, Listening and Speaking.** Each is weighted equally, at one fifth of the total.

**Reading and Use of English is one paper carrying two of those five components.** That is why it is printed at 40% while the other papers are worth 20% each - and it is why Listening and Speaking, with no percentage printed beside them, are each worth exactly as much as Writing.

**What this changes in practice.** Use of English is not a supporting skill on this examination; it is a fifth of your grade in its own right, and it is the component most candidates treat as grammar practice to be fitted in around the reading. An hour a week on Use of English is worth the same as an hour a week on Speaking, and more than most candidates believe.

blocks.heading: Grades and what they certify
blocks.caption: Scores as published by Cambridge English. B2 First is a B2 examination, so Grade A certifies C1 and the lowest band certifies B1.

blocks.title: Choosing between B2 First and C1 Advanced
text: A Grade A at B2 First certifies **C1** - the same level certified by a Grade C at C1 Advanced. If C1 is what you need and you are on the boundary, that is a genuine choice rather than a trick.

**The honest test:** enter the level you can already nearly reach. These are level examinations, not banded tests. Entering a level far above you produces a low certificate or none, not a stretched performance.
**And the safety net is real.** A score between 140 and 159 on B2 First still certifies B1. You do not walk away with nothing.

parts.heading: Reading and Use of English: 1 hour 15 minutes, 7 parts, 52 questions
bullets: **Seventy-five minutes for fifty-two questions is under ninety seconds each**, and this paper carries two of your five component scores. It is the tightest paper on the examination for time.
**Split your practice the way the marks split.** The Use of English parts and the Reading parts are scored separately, so working only through reading passages leaves a fifth of your grade untouched.
**The Use of English parts reward precision, not comprehension.** You can understand a sentence perfectly and still lose the mark on the form of the word. Learn word families, not just meanings.
**Transfer answers as you go** if you are allowed to, rather than leaving it to the end.
**Never leave a blank.** No penalty for a wrong answer means a blank is the only guaranteed nought on the paper.

parts.heading: Writing: 1 hour 20 minutes, 2 parts
bullets: **Part 1 is compulsory and Part 2 is one from four.** Read all five prompts before you choose, and choose on which gives you material rather than which topic you like.
**Forty minutes each.** Plan for five, write for thirty, check for five. The check is worth more than the extra paragraph.

**The task tells you the reader and the purpose.** Both are assessed. An essay, a review, an email and a report do not open the same way, and the first sentence should already sound like the right one.
**Cover every content point.** Part 1 in particular sets specific points to address, and missing one caps the content mark however well the rest is written.
**Range is assessed as well as accuracy.** A safe, simple piece with no errors scores below an ambitious one with a few - but not below a careless one.

parts.heading: Listening: about 40 minutes, 4 parts, 30 questions
bullets: **A full fifth of your grade, in forty minutes.** Treat it as a paper, not as revision you do while tired.
**You hear everything twice.** First listening for the answer, second for the gaps - do not try to be certain on the first pass.
**Read ahead in the pauses.** Knowing what is being asked is most of the work.
**Answer every question before the second listening ends**, even if you are unsure. An answer you revise beats a blank you run out of time for.
Practise with a range of accents, not only the one your teacher has.

parts.heading: Speaking: 14 minutes per pair, 4 parts
bullets: **A fifth of the qualification, in fourteen minutes, with a partner.** The interaction is assessed, not just your English.
**Part 2 is a long turn.** Practise speaking for a full minute without stopping, on a picture you have not seen before. Most candidates have never once done this out loud before the day.
**Do not answer the question you prepared.** Examiners recognise rehearsed material instantly, and it scores below genuine hesitant speech.
**Engage with your partner in the collaborative parts** - agree, disagree, ask them something. Two monologues score below one conversation.
**Keep going when you make a mistake.** Self-correction is credited; stopping is not.

hero.text: The level most universities mean when they ask for proof of academic English. Four papers, five scored components, and no weighting printed beside any of them.

blocks.title: Where these figures come from
text: Papers, durations, parts and questions were read from Cambridge English's own [C1 Advanced exam format page](https://www.cambridgeenglish.org/exams-and-tests/advanced/exam-format/). The grade table was read from Cambridge's [results page](https://www.cambridgeenglish.org/exams-and-tests/qualifications/results/).

**A note on the weightings.** Cambridge's C1 Advanced format page prints **no percentage against any paper**. The five-component model below is Cambridge's own published scoring method, and it is stated here as that rather than as a figure taken from the format page.

Cambridge materials are linked, never copied. No question, task or mark-scheme wording is reproduced; the methods on this page are RCF English's own. **RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Cambridge English.**

blocks.heading: The four papers
rows: 15 minutes per pair of candidates; 23 minutes per group of three

blocks.title: Five scored components, equally weighted
text: As at B2 First, the overall result is **the average of five component scores: Reading, Use of English, Writing, Listening and Speaking**, each weighted equally at one fifth.

**Reading and Use of English is one paper carrying two of those five.** At this level it runs to eight parts and fifty-six questions in ninety minutes - one more part and four more questions than at B2 First, in fifteen more minutes.

**Listening and Speaking are each worth as much as Writing**, despite Writing taking ninety minutes and Speaking fifteen. Time spent in the examination hall is not a guide to what a component is worth.

blocks.heading: Grades and what they certify
blocks.caption: Scores as published by Cambridge English. C1 Advanced is a C1 examination, so Grade A certifies C2 and the lowest certificated band certifies B2.
rows: Reported on the Statement of Results only

blocks.title: The bottom row is the one to read carefully
text: C1 Advanced is the first level on this ladder where a score can leave you **without a certificate at all**. Cambridge reports scores between 142 and 159 on the Statement of Results, but no certificate is issued for them.

At B1 Preliminary and B2 First every band in the published table produces a certificate of some level. At C1 Advanced that stops being true, which is a reason to be honest with yourself about readiness before entering.

parts.heading: Reading and Use of English: 1 hour 30 minutes, 8 parts, 56 questions
bullets: **Ninety minutes, fifty-six questions, two of your five component scores.** Budget the time part by part before the day, not during it.

**The Use of English parts at this level test precision under pressure** - word formation, collocation, and the exact structure a sentence needs. Reading widely helps; reading widely is not sufficient.
**The long reading parts reward locating rather than absorbing.** You are matching claims against text, not studying it. Read the questions first.
**Leave nothing blank.** There is no penalty for a wrong answer.
This is the paper where candidates most often run out of time, and the last part is worth as much as the first.

parts.heading: Writing: 1 hour 30 minutes, 2 parts
bullets: **Forty-five minutes each.** At this level a plan is not optional - the difference between a C and a B is usually structure rather than vocabulary.
**Part 1 is compulsory** and typically asks you to weigh points from given input. **Evaluate, do not summarise.** Repeating the input in your own words answers half the task.
**Part 2 offers a choice.** Choose on which form you can hold - a proposal, a report, a review and a letter each have a register, and the register is assessed.
**A C1 essay has a position.** Balanced does not mean uncommitted. Say what you think and defend it.
**Leave five minutes per piece to check.** Accuracy is assessed at this level with less tolerance than below it.

parts.heading: Listening: about 40 minutes, 4 parts, 30 questions
bullets: **A fifth of your grade in forty minutes**, and at C1 the recordings are longer and the distractors are better.

**The wrong answer is usually mentioned aloud.** At this level the speaker often says the thing that is not the answer, and the correct option is paraphrased rather than quoted. Listen for meaning, not for matching words.
**Everything is heard twice.** Use the first pass for the straightforward questions and the second for the two or three that are doing the discriminating.
Practise with unscripted speech - interviews, discussions, lectures - rather than only with course recordings.

parts.heading: Speaking: 15 minutes per pair, 4 parts
bullets: **A fifth of the qualification in fifteen minutes**, and the part most candidates prepare least.

**The collaborative task is where C1 is shown.** You are expected to negotiate, build on what your partner says, disagree politely and reach or fail to reach a decision. Agreeing pleasantly with everything scores low.
**Develop, do not list.** At C1 an answer is expected to have a reason, a qualification or an example attached to it.
**Hesitation is not fatal; silence is.** Fillers, self-correction and rephrasing all read as competence at this level.
**Rehearsed answers are audible.** Prepare topics and structures, not sentences.
